title: Azure Policy: guardrails inherited down the hierarchy

videos.script: Azure Policy is not about who may do something. It is about what may exist. {{what}} Bia may own the whole subscription, and still be refused a machine in Texas. The rule is about Texas, not about her. {{texas}} A policy has two halves. The definition is a condition and an effect: if the location is not Brazil, deny. {{definition}} The assignment puts that definition on a scope, and it holds for everything below. {{tree}} Nothing below can switch it off. Several rules add up, and the strictest one wins. {{cumulative}} You will read Microsoft's own definitions, straight from where it publishes them. {{github}} Then you will write the shop's two rules in Bicep, and see one string that two different evaluators read. {{brackets}} Effects run in a fixed order. Change before deny, deny before audit. {{order}} And a deny only acts on a request. What already exists is reported, not removed. {{end}}
